query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The as‐cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi exhibits favorable plasticity and machinability due to its highly disordered, simple solid‐solution state that permits easy dislocation glide, but this same disorder leads to relatively low hardness and strength because there are few local obstacles to dislocation movement. Promoting short‐range atomic ordering (SRO) via controlled thermal aging introduces local lattice distortions that act as effective dislocation pinning sites, thereby increasing hardness and yield strength while reducing ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its as‐cast, disordered simple solid‐solution state with relatively large grain sizes and minimal SRO.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to a controlled thermal aging treatment at 500–600 °C for varying durations (e.g., 1–10 hours) to promote the formation of short‐range atomic ordering (SRO) without inducing significant precipitation or phase separation.
generation.conditions: Thermal aging at 500–600 °C followed by quasi‐static mechanical compression testing at 25 °C and elevated temperatures up to 600 °C. Microstructural characterization (e.g., high-resolution XRD or atom probe tomography) is employed to monitor the extent of SRO.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of SRO regions that create localized lattice distortions, which serve as obstacles to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: In the as‐cast state, the random distribution of atoms allows dislocations to glide easily, enabling high plasticity and machinability but yielding low strength. Thermal aging initiates SRO, enhancing lattice distortion and effectively pinning dislocations. This increased dislocation impediment raises the material’s hardness and yield strength while reducing ductility in a predictable and controllable manner.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will exhibit a measurable increase in hardness and compressive yield strength relative to the as‐cast material, with a corresponding moderate decrease in ductility. The degree of strengthening will correlate with the extent of SRO detected by microstructural analyses.
generation.baseline: As‐cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi characterized by low hardness and yield strength but high plasticity and machinability due to its fully disordered solid‐solution state.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to equimolar and near‐equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloys in the simple solid‐solution state when aged at temperatures between 500 and 600 °C. Outside these thermal conditions (e.g., at significantly higher temperatures or prolonged durations that might induce unwanted precipitation), the mechanism may shift from SRO‐induced strengthening to other forms of precipitation hardening, which are not addressed here.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the extent of SRO and the improvement in mechanical properties needs to be established. It is also uncertain how the balance between increased strength and reduced ductility will evolve with different aging durations or slightly varied thermal conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples: one set in the as‐cast state and one set subjected to controlled thermal aging at 500–600 °C for durations ranging from 1 to 10 hours. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (using high-resolution XRD, atom probe tomography, or TEM) to quantify the extent of SRO and monitor for any precipitation. Conduct quasi‐static compression tests at 25 °C and elevated temperatures up to 600 °C to measure hardness, yield strength, and ductility.
measurements: Extent of SRO (via atom probe tomography or high-resolution XRD)
Grain size and any secondary phase formation (via TEM/EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If controlled thermal aging does not produce a consistent increase in hardness and yield strength in correlation with the extent of SRO, or if any observed strengthening is instead clearly attributable to precipitation rather than SRO, then the hypothesis would be falsified. Furthermore, if the aging treatment fails to alter the mechanical properties significantly while SRO can be confirmed, the proposed mechanism would be called into question.

cited_evidence.text: The as-cast Al15Hf25Nb32Ti28 exhibits a single B2 phase (Fig. 3D) with weak B2-LRO indicated by the magnified B2-(111) and (210) peak in the inset of Fig. 3A. TEM-SAED (Fig. 3H) further confirms the B2-LRO. The compression test (Fig. 4A) exhibits a σYS of 1.5 GPa. Notably, the samples endured up to a 50% height reduction without fracture before the test termination, demonstrating exceptional plasticity. Compared to Al25Hf25Nb25Ti25 and Al20Hf24Nb29Ti27, Al15Hf25Nb32Ti28 experiences a marginal σYS reduction by ~ 10%, but a notable εf increase. Concurrently, B2-LRO is further weakened to be nearly XRD undetectable, suggesting that LRO exerts a more pronounced effect on plasticity rather than strength. The MC studies in Fig. 5 (A and E) show a Ttransform of ~1150 K, around half of the predicted Tmelt of ~2208 K. The limited atomic mobility and diffusion at Ttransform lead to only a minimal LRO establishment, estimated to be ~33% of the reference state at 0 K.

However, the application of these precipitation strengthening models requires knowledge of a number of parameters, including: the degree of short-range ordering as a function of thermal treatment; the size and spacing of the short-range ordered regions; the lattice misfit between the BCC and B2 phases (requiring high resolution X-ray diffraction measurements); the elastic properties of the BCC and B2 phases; interfacial and fault energies; and the volume fraction of the B2 precipitates. While simple approximations may suffice for some of these parameters in less complicated alloys, these parameters can vary a great deal in the current RHEA, and the approximations are likely to give large uncertainties. Additional scientific studies are therefore required to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions (especially to the B2 phase) on the multitude of parameters that can influence precipitation strengthening in these complex RHEAs. proposals.material_system: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its as‐cast simple solid-solution state
proposals.intervention: Apply controlled thermal aging to promote short-range atomic ordering (SRO) without full precipitation
proposals.conditions: Aging treatment at 500–600 °C for varying durations (e.g., 1–10 hours); mechanical compression tests conducted from 25 °C up to 600 °C under quasi‐static loading
proposals.structural_mediator: Development of SRO regions that locally enhance lattice distortions
proposals.mechanism: In the as‐cast state the nearly random solid solution offers high dislocation mobility yielding good plasticity and machinability but limited obstacles to dislocation motion; thermal aging promotes SRO that increases local lattice distortions and dislocation pinning, thereby raising hardness and strength
proposals.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will show increased hardness and compressive strength (and a corresponding reduction in ductility) relative to the as‐cast baseline; the magnitude of the increase should correlate with the extent of SRO formation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This hypothesis directly links the balance between high plasticity (from disordered, low pinning) and low hardness/strength to the absence of strengthening features (such as SRO) in the as-cast state; a controlled aging treatment would provide a direct test of whether promoting SRO can alter the deformation behavior

proposals.material_system: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state
proposals.intervention: Introduce an aging heat-treatment designed to precipitate nanoscale coherent B2-like (or other intermetallic) precipitates
proposals.conditions: Aging at ~600 °C for 2–6 hours followed by natural aging at room temperature; compressive and hardness tests performed at 25 °C and up to 600 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent precipitates embedded in the disordered matrix
proposals.mechanism: The simple solid-solution state lacks fine precipitates that could obstruct dislocation glide; controlled precipitate formation increases the density of obstacles, thereby enhancing yield strength and hardness while potentially sacrificing some ductility
proposals.predicted_outcome: Post-aging samples will exhibit the emergence of nanoscale precipitates (detectable via TEM/atom probe), with a corresponding increase in hardness and compressive yield strength compared to the unaged alloy; if precipitates grow too coarse, embrittlement may occur
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By establishing whether nanoscale precipitates can strengthen CoCrFeNiTi without excessively impairing ductility, one can test if the lack of such features is responsible for its relatively low hardness and strength despite good plasticity

proposals.material_system: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in as-cast state versus a refined-grain version of the same alloy
proposals.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation (e.g., equal-channel angular pressing, ECAE) to induce ultrafine grain structures and high dislocation densities
proposals.conditions: Process samples by ECAE at room temperature to achieve grain sizes below 1 μm; subsequent compressive tests under quasi-static load at 25 °C and moderate elevated temperatures up to 600 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain refinement and increased internal dislocation network density
proposals.mechanism: The as-cast solid solution may allow easy dislocation glide due to relatively large grains, yielding high plasticity; refining the microstructure introduces grain-boundary strengthening (Hall-Petch effect) and additional dislocation obstacles, thereby increasing yield strength and hardness
proposals.predicted_outcome: ECAE-processed samples will show a significant increase in hardness and compressive strength relative to the coarse-grained baseline, with potential modest trade-offs in ductility; microstructural analysis will reveal refined grains and dense dislocation structures
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This lever tests whether the low hardness and strength are inherently due to the coarse microstructure of the simple solid solution, thereby isolating the effect of grain size and dislocation density on the deformation behavior

proposals.material_system: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi tested in its as-cast state
proposals.intervention: Perform systematic high strain-rate mechanical testing across temperatures to evaluate strain rate sensitivity
proposals.conditions: Conduct compressive loading experiments at 25 °C and 600 °C with strain rates spanning several orders of magnitude (e.g., 10^(-4) s^-1 to 10^1 s^-1)
proposals.structural_mediator: Activation of thermally activated dislocation motion and possible dynamic strain aging events
proposals.mechanism: The low hardness and strength may be due to a low intrinsic barrier for thermally activated dislocation glide in the simple solid-solution state; varying the strain rate can modify the balance between dislocation speed and obstacle activation, thereby revealing whether dynamic strain rate sensitivity controls the deformation
proposals.predicted_outcome: At higher strain rates, the alloy is predicted to display increased hardness and yield stress due to dislocation trapping and reduced time for recovery processes, whereas at lower strain rates the alloy will mainly deform by easy dislocation glide; an abnormal strain rate sensitivity (compared to similar HEAs) would support the mechanism
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By isolating the effect of strain rate on mechanical response, this approach directly tests the hypothesis that the combination of good plasticity and low hardness/strength is governed by easy thermally activated dislocation motion in the absence of significant obstacles

decision.rationale: Direction C is selected because it directly tests the idea that the relatively low hardness and strength of as‐cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is due to the lack of short‐range atomic ordering (SRO), which normally provides local lattice distortions that hinder dislocation motion. In the as‐cast state, the high degree of disorder favors easy dislocation glide (yielding good plasticity and machinability) but with few obstacles to strengthen the material. By applying a controlled thermal aging treatment designed to promote SRO without full precipitation, one can directly correlate the development of local ordering with increases in hardness and yield strength. This approach both explains the current anomalous combination of properties and provides a clear, testable intervention. The available literature shows that alterations in microstructural features (grain boundaries, ordering, and precipitates) are central to modulating dislocation mobility and strengthening, and aging treatments have been successfully used in similar alloy systems to manipulate these features.
